To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the standard analysis for TLS data, treating the data as an SRS from the target population, is likely to be substantially biased and that weighting and using sample survey software to estimate standard errors is a better approach to analyzing TLS data.

(1) TLS is a valuable method for studying a population that is difficult to sample by other methods, (2) the analysis of TLS data should be conducted using sample survey software to account for the clustering within locations, (3) the weights should be calculated based on the inverse probability of sampling, and (4) data on the frequency of location attendance are needed to calculate these weights accurately.
time-location sampling is useful for collecting data on a hard-to-achieve population and that, if analyzed appropriately, it can yield unbiased estimates and valid estimates of uncertainty.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, for the analysis of data collected by TLS, the use of a weighting procedure that takes account of the sampling probability and the clustering of sampling units is preferable to the assumption of a SRS.
the analysis of TLS data should be done as a two-stage survey with weights based on the inverse probability of being sampled.

the analysis of TLS data should be conducted using a weighting procedure that adjusts for the probability of being sampled and using sample-survey analysis methods that account for the clustering within sampling locations and the variability in the weights.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

TLS can be used as an alternative to RDS to study hard-to-reach populations and, if used, can be analyzed in a straightforward way that yields more precise estimates of associations between variables of interest than an analysis assuming an SRS.
TLS is an efficient method of obtaining information from a hidden population, provided that the data are analyzed using appropriate statistical methods.

, for studies of populations that can be sampled by time–location methods, these are likely to be a better choice than respondent-driven sampling, because of their greater efficiency and their ability to provide unbiased estimates of population prevalence and association parameters, and because they can be analyzed using standard statistical software for two-stage sample surveys.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TLS data should be analyzed as a sample survey, using appropriate software and taking account of clustering within locations and variation in the probability that a person attends locations.
TLS data should be analyzed as a cluster sample survey with weights, and that the weights should be based on the inverse probability of being sampled.
, when the population of interest is the source population for the TLS, the data should be analyzed as a sample survey.
